{{Short description|Theorem in projective geometry}}
{{more footnotes|date=March 2016}}
[[File:Oval-def-fin.svg|thumb|to the definition of a finite oval: <math>t</math> tangent, <math>s_1,...s_n</math> secants, <math>n</math> is the order of the projective plane (number of points on a line -1)]]
In [[projective geometry]], '''Segre's theorem''', named after the Italian [[mathematician]] [[Beniamino Segre]], is the statement:
*Any [[Oval (projective plane)|oval]] in a ''finite [[Pappus's hexagon theorem|pappian]]'' [[projective plane]] of ''odd'' order is a nondegenerate projective [[conic section]].

This statement was assumed 1949 by the two Finnish mathematicians [[Gustaf Järnefelt|G. Järnefelt]] and [[Paul Kustaanheimo|P. Kustaanheimo]] and its proof was published in 1955 by B. Segre.

A finite pappian projective plane can be imagined as the projective closure of the real plane (by a [[line at infinity]]), where the [[real numbers]] are replaced by a [[finite field]] {{mvar|K}}. ''Odd order'' means that {{math|1={{!}}''K''{{!}} = ''n''}} is odd. An oval is a curve similar to a [[circle]] (see definition below): any line meets it in at most 2 points and through any point of it there is exactly one tangent. The standard examples are the nondegenerate projective conic sections.

In pappian projective planes of ''even'' order greater than four there are ovals which are not conics. In an infinite plane there exist ovals, which are not conics. In the real plane one just glues a half of a circle and a suitable [[ellipse]] [[smoothness|smoothly]].

The proof of Segre's theorem, shown below, uses the 3-point version of [[Pascal theorem|Pascal's theorem]] and a property of a finite field of odd order, namely, that the product of all the nonzero elements equals -1.

== Definition of an oval ==
{{main|Oval (projective plane)}}
*In a projective plane a set <math>\mathfrak o</math> of points is called '''oval''', if:
:(1) Any line <math>g</math> meets <math>\mathfrak o</math> in at most two points.
If <math>|g\cap\mathfrak o|=0</math> the line <math>g</math> is an ''exterior'' (or ''passing'') line; in case <math>|g\cap\mathfrak o|=1</math> a ''tangent line'' and if <math>|g\cap\mathfrak o|=2</math> the line is a ''secant line''.
:(2) For any point <math>P \in \mathfrak o</math> there exists exactly one tangent <math>t</math> at {{mvar|P}}, i.e., <math> t\cap\mathfrak o=\{P\}</math>.

For ''finite'' planes (i.e. the set of points is finite) we have a more convenient characterization:
* For a finite projective plane of ''order'' {{mvar|n}} (i.e. any line contains {{math|''n'' + 1}} points) a set <math>\mathfrak o</math> of points is an oval [[if and only if]] <math>|\mathfrak o|=n+1</math> and no three points are [[collinear]] (on a common line).

== Pascal's 3-point version ==
[[File:Pascal-3p.svg|thumb|for the proof <math>g_\infty</math> is the tangent at <math>P_3</math>]]
;Theorem:
Let be <math>\mathfrak o</math> an oval in a pappian projective plane of [[Characteristic (algebra)|characteristic]] <math>\ne 2</math>. <br />
<math>\mathfrak o</math> is a nondegenerate conic if and only if statement '''(P3)'''
holds:
 
:'''(P3): ''' Let be <math>P_1,P_2,P_3</math> any triangle on <math>\mathfrak o</math> and <math>\overline {P_iP_i}</math> the tangent at point <math>P_i</math> to <math>\mathfrak o</math>, then the points 
:::<math>P_4:= \overline {P_1P_1} \cap \overline {P_2P_3},\  P_5:= \overline {P_2P_2} \cap \overline {P_1P_3}, \ P_6:= \overline {P_3P_3} \cap \overline {P_1P_2}</math> 
:::are collinear.<ref>E. Hartmann: ''[http://www.mathematik.tu-darmstadt.de/~ehartmann/circlegeom.pdf Planar Circle Geometries, an Introduction to Moebius-, Laguerre- and Minkowski Planes.]'' Skript, TH Darmstadt (PDF; 891&nbsp;kB), p.&nbsp;34.</ref>

[[File:Pascal-3p-proof.svg|thumb|to the proof of the 3-point Pascal theorem]]
;Proof:
Let the projective plane be coordinatized [[Homogeneous coordinates|inhomogeneously]] over a field <math>K</math> 
such that <math>P_3=(0), \; g_\infty</math> is the tangent at <math>P_3 , \ (0,0) \in \mathfrak o</math>, the x-axis is the tangent at the point <math>(0,0)</math>  and  <math>\mathfrak o</math> contains the point <math>(1,1)</math>. Furthermore, we set <math>P_1=(x_1,y_1), \; P_2=(x_2,y_2)\ .</math> (s. image)<br />
The oval <math>\mathfrak o</math> can be described by a function <math>f: K \mapsto K</math> such that:
:<math>\mathfrak o=\{(x,y)\in K^2 \;|\; y=f(x)\} \ \cup \{(\infty)\}\; .</math>
The tangent at point <math>(x_0,f(x_0))</math> will be described using a function <math>f' </math> such that its equation is
:<math>y=f'(x_0)(x-x_0) +f(x_0)</math> 
Hence (s. image)
:<math>P_5=(x_1,f'(x_2)(x_1-x_2)+f(x_2))</math> and  <math>P_4=(x_2,f'(x_1)(x_2-x_1)+f(x_1))\; .</math>
'''I:''' if <math>\mathfrak o</math> is a non [[degenerate conic]] we have <math>f(x)=x^2</math> and <math>f'(x)=2x</math> and one calculates easily that <math>P_4,P_5,P_6</math> are collinear.

'''II:''' If <math>\mathfrak o</math> is an oval with property '''(P3)''', the slope of the line <math>\overline{P_4P_5}</math> is equal to the slope of the line <math>\overline{P_1P_2}</math>, that means:
:<math>f'(x_2)+f'(x_1) - \frac{f(x_2)-f(x_1)}{x_2-x_1}=\frac{f(x_2)-f(x_1)}{x_2-x_1}</math> and hence
:'''(i):''' <math> (f'(x_2)+f'(x_1))(x_2-x_1)=2(f(x_2)-f(x_1))</math> for all  <math>x_1,x_2 \in K</math>. 
With <math>f(0)=f'(0)=0</math>  one gets
:(ii): <math>f'(x_2)x_2=2f(x_2)</math> and from <math>f(1)=1</math> we get 
:(iii): <math>f'(1)=2 \; .</math> 
(i) and (ii) yield
:(iv): <math>f'(x_2)x_1=f'(x_1)x_2</math> and with (iii) at least we get 
:(v): <math>f'(x_2)=2x_2</math> for all <math>x_2 \in K</math>. 
A consequence of (ii) and (v) is   
:<math>f(x_2)=x_2^2, \; x_2 \in K</math>. 
Hence <math>\mathfrak o</math> is a nondegenerate conic.

''Remark:''
Property (P3) is fulfilled for any oval in a pappian projective plane of characteristic '''2''' with a nucleus (all tangents meet at the nucleus). Hence in this case (P3) is also true for non-conic ovals.<ref>E. Hartmann: ''[http://www.mathematik.tu-darmstadt.de/~ehartmann/circlegeom.pdf Planar Circle Geometries, an Introduction to Moebius-, Laguerre- and Minkowski Planes.]'' Skript, TH Darmstadt (PDF; 891&nbsp;kB), p.&nbsp;35.</ref>

== Segre's theorem and its proof ==
;Theorem:
Any oval <math>\mathfrak o</math> in a ''finite pappian'' projective plane of ''odd'' order is a nondegenerate conic section.
[[File:Pascal-3p.svg|thumb|3-point version of Pascal's theorem, for the proof we assume <math>g_\infty=\overline{P_2P_3}</math>]]
[[File:Segre-proof.svg|thumb|Segre's theorem: to its proof]]
;Proof:<ref>E. Hartmann: ''[http://www.mathematik.tu-darmstadt.de/~ehartmann/circlegeom.pdf Planar Circle Geometries, an Introduction to Moebius-, Laguerre- and Minkowski Planes.]'' Skript, TH Darmstadt (PDF; 891&nbsp;kB), p.&nbsp;41.</ref>
For the proof we show that the oval has property '''(P3)''' of the 3-point version of Pascal's theorem.

Let be <math>P_1,P_2,P_3</math> any triangle on <math>\mathfrak o</math> and <math>P_4,P_5,P_6</math> defined as described in '''(P3)'''. 
The pappian plane will be coordinatized inhomogeneously over a finite field 
<math>K</math>, such that<math>P_3=(\infty),\; P_2=(0),\; P_1=(1,1)</math> and <math> (0,0)</math> is the common point of the tangents at <math>P_2</math> and <math>P_3</math>. The oval <math>\mathfrak o</math> can be described using a [[bijective]] function <math>f: K^*:=K\cup \setminus \{0\} \mapsto K^*</math>:
:<math>\mathfrak o=\{(x,y)\in K^2\; | \; y=f(x), \; x\ne 0\}\; \cup \; \{(0),(\infty)\}\; .</math>
For a point <math>P=(x,y), \; x\in K\setminus\{0,1\}</math>, the expression  <math>m(x)=\tfrac{f(x)-1}{x-1}</math> is the slope of the secant <math>\overline{PP_1}\; .</math> Because both the functions <math>x\mapsto f(x)-1</math> and <math>x\mapsto x-1</math> are bijections from
<math>K\setminus\{0,1\}</math> to <math>K\setminus\{0,-1\}</math>, and <math>x\mapsto m(x)</math> a bijection  from <math>K\setminus\{0,1\}</math> onto  <math>K\setminus\{0,m_1\}</math>, where <math>m_1</math> is the slope of the tangent at  <math>P_1</math>, for <math>K^{**}:=K\setminus\{0,1\}\; :</math>  we get
:<math>\prod_{x\in K^{**}}(f(x)-1)=\prod_{x\in K^{**}}(x-1)=1 \quad \text{und}\quad
m_1\cdot\prod_{x\in K^{**}}\frac{f(x)-1}{x-1}=-1\; .</math>
(Remark: For <math>K^*:= K\setminus\{0\}</math> we have: 
<math>\displaystyle \prod_{k\in K^*}k=-1\; .</math>)<br />
Hence
:<math>-1=m_1\cdot\prod_{x\in K^{**}}\frac{f(x)-1}{x-1}=
m_1\cdot\frac{
\displaystyle \prod_{x\in K^{**}}(f(x)-1)}{
\displaystyle \prod_{x\in K^{**}}(x-1)}=m_1\; .</math>
Because the slopes of line <math>\overline{P_5P_6}</math>  and tangent
<math>\overline{P_1P_1}</math> both are <math>-1</math>, it follows that
<math>\overline{P_1P_1}\cap \overline{P_2P_3}=P_4 \in\overline{P_5P_6} </math>.
This is true for any triangle <math>P_1,P_2,P_3 \in \mathfrak o</math>.

So: '''(P3)''' of the 3-point Pascal theorem holds and the oval is a non degenerate conic.
